name: Primary Hyperaldosteronism

prevalence.estimate: 5-10% of hypertensive patients; 1 in 1,000 general population

ethnicAssociations: African American (higher prevalence among hypertensive patients)

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines for Primary Aldosteronism

criteria.description: Elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) >30 ng/dL per ng/mL/h (or equivalent units) as screening test
Confirmatory test positive: failure to suppress aldosterone after saline infusion test, oral sodium loading, fludrocortisone suppression test, or captopril challenge test
Subtype differentiation by adrenal CT and/or adrenal venous sampling (AVS)
Suppressed or undetectable plasma renin activity (PRA) or direct renin concentration

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Positive ARR screening followed by confirmatory suppression testing demonstrating autonomous aldosterone production
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Most patients with primary aldosteronism are normokalemic. Hypokalemia is present in only ~30% of cases. Subtypes include aldosterone-producing adenoma (APA, ~35%), bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (BAH, ~60%), and rare forms (unilateral hyperplasia, adrenal carcinoma, familial hyperaldosteronism).

pathognomonic.notes: Classic presentation but hypokalemia present in only ~30%; resistant HTN is the most common indication for screening

common.symptomName: Hypertension (often moderate to severe, resistant to treatment)

common.notes: Due to hypokalemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

laboratory: Elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) as screening test
Suppressed plasma renin activity (PRA) or direct renin concentration
Failure of aldosterone suppression on confirmatory testing
imaging: CT adrenals: may show unilateral adenoma (usually <2 cm) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
CT may be normal in microadenomas
Adrenal venous sampling (AVS) is gold standard for lateralization
Echocardiography may show LVH disproportionate to degree of hypertension
genetic: Familial hyperaldosteronism type I (glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism): CYP11B1/CYP11B2 chimeric gene
Familial hyperaldosteronism type II: CLCN2 mutations
Familial hyperaldosteronism type III: KCNJ5 mutations
Somatic KCNJ5 mutations found in ~40% of aldosterone-producing adenomas
ATP1A1, ATP2B3, CACNA1D somatic mutations also identified
other: Adrenal venous sampling (AVS) for subtype differentiation before surgical decision
Saline infusion test (250 mL/h x 4 hours; PAC >10 ng/dL confirms PA)
ECG may show signs of hypokalemia (U waves, ST depression, prolonged QT)

distinguishingFeatures: Cushing has elevated cortisol with characteristic phenotype
Cushing may cause hypokalemia but from different mechanism
Moon facies, striae, and proximal weakness in Cushing
Renovascular hypertension has elevated renin (secondary hyperaldosteronism)
ARR typically not elevated (both renin and aldosterone high)
Liddle syndrome has low aldosterone and low renin

redFlags: Severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mEq/L) with cardiac arrhythmias
Adrenal mass >4 cm (concern for adrenocortical carcinoma)
Young-onset hypertension (<20 years) suggesting familial hyperaldosteronism
Flash pulmonary edema with bilateral renal artery stenosis mimicking PA
Concurrent adrenal incidentaloma requiring functional workup
references: Funder JW, et al. The Management of Primary Aldosteronism: Case Detection, Diagnosis, and Treatment: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2016;101(5):1889-916.
Young WF. Primary aldosteronism: renaissance of a syndrome. Clin Endocrinol (Oxf). 2007;66(5):607-18.
Monticone S, et al. Prevalence and Clinical Manifestations of Primary Aldosteronism Encountered in Primary Care Practice. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2017;69(14):1811-1820.
Stowasser M. Update in primary aldosteronism. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2015;100(1):1-10.
